Chapter 3: Reclaiming Personal Power and Practicing Self-Care
Now that you've started setting boundaries, the next step is all about turning your focus inward—reclaiming your sense of power and making self-care a priority.
When you’re living with the emotional ups and downs of someone else—especially if they have borderline personality disorder—it’s easy to lose sight of your own needs. You might find yourself so wrapped up in their moods and struggles, you end up putting yourself last without even realizing it.
Reclaiming your personal power means something simple, but powerful: realizing you have choices. You can set limits. You can take actions that support your own well-being. And, just to be clear, this isn’t about controlling the person with BPD. It’s about taking charge of your own life, and doing what you need to feel healthy and whole.
Self-care really is the foundation of this process. And I know… sometimes it feels selfish, or even impossible, to focus on yourself when there’s so much drama swirling around. But here’s something to pay attention to—self-care isn’t a luxury. It’s a necessity, especially if you’re navigating the challenges of a relationship affected by BPD.
So, what does self-care and empowerment actually look like? Let’s talk about a few ways you can put this into practice.
First, make time for regular reflection. That could mean journaling, meditation, or just a quiet walk where you check in with how you’re really feeling. It’s about reconnecting with yourself, even if it’s just for a few minutes.
Next, don’t be afraid to reach out for support. Whether it’s friends, support groups, or talking to a professional, having people who understand what you’re going through can make a world of difference. Sharing your experiences helps break that sense of isolation, and sometimes, just knowing you’re not alone is a huge relief.
Another important step is to set realistic expectations. You can’t fix or change the person with BPD—no matter how much you love them. What you can control is your own response, your choices, and how you take care of yourself.
Then there’s practicing assertiveness. This means expressing your needs and feelings honestly, not with aggression or apology, but with clarity and respect. Think of it as finding that healthy middle ground between being passive and being hostile.
And finally, make time for joy. Seriously—schedule things that bring you happiness outside of the BPD dynamic. Whether it’s a hobby, meeting up with friends, or just doing something creative, these moments remind you who you are beyond the relationship.
Picture this: maybe you’ve stopped seeing your friends or dropped your favorite activities because there’s always a crisis at home. Reclaiming your power might mean telling your partner you’re going out with friends—yes, even if it feels awkward or brings up their anxiety. It’s tough at first, but it’s an important step toward finding balance and respecting yourself again.
Now, let’s talk about guilt and self-blame. It’s so common to feel like you’re responsible for your partner’s happiness or stability. But here’s the truth: that belief isn’t just unrealistic—it’s actually harmful. Each of us is responsible for our own feelings and actions.
Letting go of guilt is about realizing that taking care of yourself isn’t a betrayal. In fact, it’s the only way you’ll have the strength and resilience to support anyone else. Think of it like those airplane safety instructions—put your own oxygen mask on first before helping others.
Reclaiming your personal power isn’t a one-time thing. It’s an ongoing journey. It takes courage, self-compassion, and a willingness to challenge old habits. But over time, you’ll find you can show up in your relationship from a place of strength—instead of fear or obligation.
